title.narrative: Output 7.3. Increased capacity of Member States to set adequate wages and promote decent working time

description.narrative:
1. The Department of Labour Welfare, Government of Assam in India reconstituted the composition of the tripartite minimum wage advisory committee to make it more inclusive and broad-based by giving representation to the informal sector workers (i.e., domestic workers and transport workers) and enterprises (i.e., women entrepreneurs) for the first time through notification. ILO representatives were also included in the committee as special invitee for providing technical support.
2. The Department of Labour Welfare, Government of Assam in India conducted two meetings of the strengthened minimum wage advisory committee (after a gap of seven years) to set new minimum wage levels through evidence-based consultation. Although the regulation (i.e., the Minimum Wages Act, 1948) provides for considering the needs of the workers and their families only while setting the minimum wage rates, the committee unanimously further decided to consider economic factors including productivity in line with ILO’s Convention 131 so that minimum wages are fixed at an adequate and balanced level. Accordingly, ILO has initiated an evidence-based scientific study with the supervision, monitoring and approval of the committee. It is expected that the new minimum wage levels will be notified by December 2023.
3. As per ILO’s advice, the Government of Assam, and the Minimum Wage Advisory Committee, during the discussion of the committee has decided to extend the general minimum wages (of unskilled workers) to the domestic workers of the state as well thereby ensuring wage parity. In order to give effects to this decision, Government has decided to merge the minimum wage board for domestic workers with the general minimum wage board and accordingly, the composition of general minimum wage board has been expanded to give representation to the domestic workers through government notification (as outlined at point 1 above). In Assam, the ILO conducted a series of consultation meetings with the highest political executives at the level of Chief Minister/Labour Ministers and senior officials involving labour secretaries and commissioners about the adoption of sound mechanism to set minimum wages and collective bargained wage rates, and their effective implementation as per Convention C131 and other relevant conventions and recommendation. This led to the issuance of administrative orders reflecting Assam state government’s collaboration with the ILO for promoting adequate wage (with wide circulation in the media).
Subsequently, ILO reached out to the social partners and organised rounds of separate discussions and presentations, which was followed by further demand from constituents for ILO technical support in strengthening wage fixing mechanism in Assam.
ILO officials as special invitees participated in two meetings of the Assam Minimum Wage Advisory Committee and rendered technical advice on the following: - Making composition of the minimum wage board more inclusive by giving adequate representation to the informal economy workers and enterprises, given the fact that minimum wage is a tool meant to protect the labour income of low paid workers, who usually work in the informal economy. This led to reconstitution of the minimum wage advisory committee. - Presentation was made before the committee on ILO principles of minimum wage system and practices around the world to develop a common understanding. Apart from others, the knowledge sharing session led to the acceptance of the importance of economic factors in wage setting process. - Presentation was made before the committee on the importance of evidence-based wage setting process through full consultation as per C131 and R135 and related indicators and methodology. As a result, the ToR for conducting an evidenced based study was approved by the advisory committee and the study is under progress.

Output 6.1. Increased capacity of Member States to promote investments in the care economy and a more balanced sharing of family responsibilities

description.narrative:
ILO tripartite constituents promoted and adopted policy recommendations for care work and care jobs for the future of decent work (e.g. NITI Aayog together with ILO publishing the 4 assessment papers, and policy recommendations, various high-level documents covering the topic of care economy – e.g. G20 Chair's Statement for the Ministerial Conference on Women's Empowerment, G20 Leaders' Declaration including gender section, with the inclusion of care economy topic).
The Government of Delhi issued a public notification with a new requirement to Placement Agencies with a view to promote improved working conditions for domestic workers.
The Ministry of Women and Child Development issued a new cost-norm for childcare workers.
Employers’ Organizations (Employers Federation of India, EFI, and All India Organization of Employers – AIOE) developed and launched voluntary code of conduct to promote decent work for domestic workers.
SEWA Kerala organized domestic workers and compiled recommendations for the Domestic Worker Legislation in Kerala. ILO has been engaging continuously with NITI Aayog to launch papers and policy brief . A stakeholder workshop was also organised on 9 May 2023 to get feedback from ILO constituents and other stakeholders such as CSO, on the Policy Brief. ILO has provided extensive comments to the Department of Labour, Govt. of NCT of Delhi on the Draft legislation on Domestic Workers in the State. There has been active engagement with Trade Unions and EBMOs, for example study to document best practices on Care Policies with EBMOs in India.
